title: Instrumentation and why they combined
summary: The band's instrumentation and working as a committee to get out of block writing.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: How did you arrive at the instrumentation for the band?
We were three trumpets, three bones, a tuba, woodwinds,
with all sorts of doubles, and a harp and keyboards, all the keyboards.

We could have gone into strings and french horns, but that was a little much, we thought. It was gilding a lily, because there was the bother of if not directly, then eventually of transporting those things. I don't know how it would have been if we had gone the other way, but this is the way we went. It might have been costs; costs usually get into those things.
The reason for the combination is that we both couldn't stand the other any longer, because of the block nature of it, where you have to write, it's just stifling.
It's all right if you don't have to do it all the time, so this was the
way we figured we could get out of it, and more than that, we didn't even know if we could get people to play it.

Bill had been in the army with Walter Rosenberger. I remember him calling Rosie down, we had dinner at the Clinton Inn one night discussing how we could do it and it wound up that Rosie and Buster, his partner at the Philharmonic, were the first percussionists (inaudible). They showed us how to do it.

It came really from a desire to--we worked the tunes out and how are we going to do these tunes is really how it was, and any idea that came up required this sort of spacing. We'd sit up in Bill's room where he worked and just talked about it, kicked it back and forth. It was a committee operation. It was a process of elimination really; we needed this to do it.
